newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU social agenda includes posted workers, social dialogue.
newsitem.headline: EU social agenda includes posted workers, social dialogue.

text.p: The European Union will finally be able to adopt the hard-fought posted workers directive and will explore issues ranging from social protection schemes to tobacco consumption during the final months of the year.
It will also try to break a longstanding deadlock over worker participation rules and debate whether to extend EU rules on working hours and rest periods to new sectors.
Following are some of the highlights of the EU's social policy agenda for the coming weeks:

POSTED WORKERS. The European Parliament is set to give a second reading this week to the hard-fought posted workers directive, clearing the way for final adoption by the September 24 Social Affairs Council.
The parliament's social affairs committee approved the Council's common position in July without amendment.
The legislation, COM(93)225, would guarantee construction and other workers who are posted across borders by their employers the same pay and working conditions as those hired locally.

Governments may wait up to one month, however, to apply minimum pay rules -- or allow trade unions and employers to negotiate such a delay. They could also exempt "small jobs" from rules on minimum wages and paid annual leave and wait up to eight days to apply the rules to assembly and installation work.

SOCIAL DIALOGUE. The Commission is set to adopt a communication on Wednesday on ways to improve the "social dialogue" -- a term referring to procedures for consulting management and labour groups or having them negotiate accords under the Social Protocol.

"We want to strengthen the social dialogue, make it more adaptable," said Barbara Nolan, spokeswoman for Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn. The communication will address issues such as efficiency and transparency, and ask the "social partners" for feedback, she said.

But it will not try to resolve complaints from groups such as UEAPME, which represents small and medium-sized businesses, who are unhappy because they have been left out of negotiations to draw up EU social policy, she said.

The EU's "big three" social partners -- the Union of Industrial and Employers' Confederations, the European Trade Union Confederation and the European Centre of Enterprises with Public Participation -- negotiated rules on parental leave that were turned into EU law. They are about to launch similar negotiation on part-time work.
The Commission continues to believe it is up to the social partners themselves to decide who their negotiating partners are, Nolan said.

WORKING TIME DIRECTIVE. The European Court of Justice is expected to rule by mid-October on Britain's challenge to the Working Time Directive, 93/104/EC, which limits the average work week to 48 hours.
The Commission will then finalise a white paper it is preparing on ways to apply the rules to sectors that were excluded from the original directive -- transport, sea work and doctors in training.
It is unhappy with the present directive, arguing that it does not need to exclude entire categories of workers.

A court advocate general issued an advisory opinion in March rejecting Britain's argument that the directive had been improperly adopted as a health and safety measure under qualified majority voting, rather than under provisions requiring unanimity.
WORKER CONSULTATION. Flynn is planning to report to the September 24 Social Affairs Council on his efforts to resolve a deadlock over EU legislation on worker consultation and participation.

The Commission is in the process of consulting member states, especially Germany, about finding a way to unblock the European Company Statute and other measures that have been stymied by disputes over worker participation.

Flynn has proposed an approach under which the EU would develop a general legal framework on informing and consulting workers -- including a measure to cover companies at national level. That would complement the existing European Works Council directive, 94/45/EC, which applies to multinational companies.

If worker consultation rules were dealt with separately, that would allow the proposed statutes for a European company, European association, European cooperative society and European mutual society to be agreed.
However, Germany, which wants its own system of "co-determination" adopted, is unhappy with the compromise because it refers only to worker "consultation", rather than "participation".

SUPPLEMENTARY PENSIONS. The Commission is waiting for a report from a high-level working party before deciding whether to resurrect a draft directive to ensure that cross-border workers take their company pension rights with them.

Flynn proposed legislation on the subject in February, but the full Commission decided to put off a decision until after hearing from the working party, headed by former French Social Affairs Minister Simone Veil, which was asked to examine barriers to the free movment of workers across the EU.

Flynn proposed that by the year 2010 EU states set a maximum limit of five years before employees are vested in their pensions. But it ran into trouble because it would have required Germany to change laws aimed at rewarding employees for long service.
The working party is expected to submit its report in February.

TELEWORKING. DGV is in the process of drafting a communication on the implications for labour laws of "teleworking" -- working from home or satellite locations rather than in traditional offices, a trend made possible because of the growth of computer and telecommunications networks.

SOCIAL PROTECTION. The Commission is planning to issue a communication, possibly in October, that will analyse the feedback it got on the communication it issued almost a year ago, COM(95)466, on the future of social protection schemes.
That communication asked national governments to consider ways to bolster their programmes for the jobless, disabled, elderly and other needy groups in the face of growing demand and tight resources.
The December 2 Social Affairs Council is tentatively set to adopt a resolution on the question.

SEX DISCRIMINATION. The December 2 Council is tentatively set to agree a draft directive that blesses schemes to boost the number of women who are hired or promoted as long as they do not turn into rigid quotas.

The measure, COM(96)93, would amend the EU's equal opportunities directive, 76/207/EEC, to clarify a European Court of Justice ruling that declared a German quota scheme illegal (the Kalanke judgment).

TOBACCO. The Commission is working on a communication that will explore ways the EU can cut tobacco consumption, looking beyond the proposal to ban tobacco advertising that has been stuck in the Health Council for several years. Flynn will present the Commission's thinking at an October 2-3 conference on tobacco and health in Helsinki, Nolan said.

CARCINOGENS. The September 24 Council is set to adopt a common position on a draft directive to amend for the first time Directive 90/394/EEC on protecting workers from risks related to exposure to carcinogens.

The legislation, COM(95)425, would set limits for exposure to benzene and extend the scope of the directive by redefining carcinogens to include products such as cosmetics, medicinal preparations and pesticides.
